# Task 1: Slate Health Check

## 1a Data quality audit and cleaning decisions

```{r}
#| label: t1-setup-and-clean
library(tidyverse)
library(gt)
library(patchwork)

DATA_PATH <- "data/movies.csv"
FOCUS <- c("Action", "Comedy", "Drama", "Horror", "Animation")

n0   <- function(x) format(round(x, 0), big.mark = ",", trim = TRUE)
n1   <- function(x) format(round(x, 1), nsmall = 1)
n2   <- function(x) format(round(x, 2), nsmall = 2)
pct1 <- function(x) sprintf("%.1f%%", x)

films_raw <- read_csv(DATA_PATH, show_col_types = FALSE)

films <- films_raw |>
  mutate(
    budget_c     = case_when(budget >= 10000 ~ budget, TRUE ~ NA_real_),
    revenue_c    = case_when(revenue > 0 ~ revenue, TRUE ~ NA_real_),
    roi_c        = revenue_c / budget_c,
    log10_budget = log10(budget_c),
    log10_roi    = log10(roi_c),
    budget_m     = budget_c / 1e6
  )

n_films     <- nrow(films_raw)
n_dup_id    <- sum(duplicated(films_raw$id))
n_dup_title <- sum(duplicated(films_raw$title))
n_bud0      <- sum(films_raw$budget == 0, na.rm = TRUE)
n_bud_small <- sum(films_raw$budget > 0 & films_raw$budget < 10000, na.rm = TRUE)
n_rev0      <- sum(films_raw$revenue == 0, na.rm = TRUE)
n_roi_na    <- sum(is.na(films_raw$roi))
same_rows   <- all(is.na(films_raw$roi) == (films_raw$budget == 0))
n_fs_na     <- sum(is.na(films_raw$franchise_status))
n_genre_na  <- sum(is.na(films_raw$primary_genre))
n_comp_na   <- sum(is.na(films_raw$primary_company)) 
n_2016      <- sum(films_raw$release_year == 2016, na.rm = TRUE)
yr_min      <- min(films_raw$release_year, na.rm = TRUE)
yr_max      <- max(films_raw$release_year, na.rm = TRUE)

genre_stats <- films |>
  group_by(primary_genre) |>
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    cov_bud = mean(!is.na(budget_c)) * 100,
    med_bud = median(budget_m, na.rm = TRUE),
    med_roi = median(roi_c, na.rm = TRUE),
    q1_roi  = quantile(roi_c, 0.25, na.rm = TRUE, names = FALSE),
    rec_pct = mean(roi_c >= 1, na.rm = TRUE) * 100,
    fra_pct = mean(franchise_status == "Franchise") * 100
  )

fs_stats <- films |>
  group_by(franchise_status) |>
  summarise(
    cov_bud = mean(!is.na(budget_c)) * 100,
    rec_pct = mean(roi_c >= 1, na.rm = TRUE) * 100
  )

dec_stats <- films |>
  filter(!is.na(release_year)) |>
  mutate(decade_num = floor(release_year / 10) * 10) |>
  group_by(decade_num) |>
  summarise(cov_bud = mean(!is.na(budget_c)) * 100)

g_stat <- function(g, stat) {
  row <- genre_stats[!is.na(genre_stats$primary_genre) & genre_stats$primary_genre == g, ]
  row[[stat]]
}

f_stat <- function(s, stat) fs_stats[[stat]][fs_stats$franchise_status == s]
d_stat <- function(d, stat) {
  row <- dec_stats[!is.na(dec_stats$decade_num) & dec_stats$decade_num == d, ]
  row[[stat]]
}


n_usable_bud <- sum(!is.na(films$budget_c))
n_usable_roi <- sum(!is.na(films$roi_c))
n_complete   <- sum(!is.na(films$budget_c) & !is.na(films$revenue_c))
n_over15     <- sum(films$roi_c > 15, na.rm = TRUE)
pct_usable_bud <- mean(!is.na(films$budget_c)) * 100
pct_usable_roi <- mean(!is.na(films$roi_c)) * 100
pct_flop       <- mean(films$roi_c < 1, na.rm = TRUE) * 100

med_budget_m  <- median(films$budget_m, na.rm = TRUE)
mean_budget_m <- mean(films$budget_m, na.rm = TRUE)
max_budget_m  <- max(films$budget_m, na.rm = TRUE)
med_roi       <- median(films$roi_c, na.rm = TRUE)
q1_roi        <- quantile(films$roi_c, .25, na.rm = TRUE, names = FALSE)
q3_roi        <- quantile(films$roi_c, .75, na.rm = TRUE, names = FALSE)
mean_roi      <- mean(films$roi_c, na.rm = TRUE)
sd_roi        <- sd(films$roi_c, na.rm = TRUE)
med_logbud    <- median(films$log10_budget, na.rm = TRUE)
sd_logbud     <- sd(films$log10_budget, na.rm = TRUE)
n_franchise   <- sum(films$franchise_status == "Franchise")

cc <- films |> filter(!is.na(budget_c), !is.na(revenue_c))
medbud_fs <- function(s) median(cc$budget_c[cc$franchise_status == s]) / 1e6
medroi_fs <- function(s) median(cc$roi_c[cc$franchise_status == s])
share_fs  <- function(s, what) (sum(cc[[what]][cc$franchise_status == s]) / sum(cc[[what]])) * 100
```

```{r}
#| include: false
#| label: tbl-t1-audit
#| tbl-cap: "Data quality audit of the raw film records."
tibble(
  Check = c("Films in the file",
            "budget = 0 (placeholder)",
            "0 < budget < USD 10,000",
            "revenue = 0 (placeholder)",
            "roi missing (= budget = 0 rows)",
            "Missing genre / company / franchise",
            "Release year range"),
  Value = c(n0(n_films),
            n0(n_bud0),
            n0(n_bud_small),
            n0(n_rev0),
            paste0(n0(n_roi_na), " (", toupper(as.character(same_rows)), ")"),
            paste(n0(n_genre_na), "/", n0(n_comp_na), "/", n0(n_fs_na)),
            paste(yr_min, "to", yr_max)),
  `% of films` = c(pct1(100),
            pct1(100 * n_bud0 / n_films),
            pct1(100 * n_bud_small / n_films),
            pct1(100 * n_rev0 / n_films),
            pct1(100 * n_roi_na / n_films),
            paste0(pct1(100 * n_genre_na / n_films), " / ",
                   pct1(100 * n_comp_na / n_films), " / ",
                   pct1(100 * n_fs_na / n_films)),
            "\u2014")
) |> gt() |>
  tab_options(
    table.font.size = "10pt",
    data_row.padding = px(4),
    column_labels.padding = px(4),
    table.width = pct(90),
    table.margin.left = px(0)
  )
```

The data audit identified missing and placeholder financial values. Zero is used throughout the file as a stand-in for "unknown": `r n0(n_bud0)` films (`r pct1(100 * n_bud0 / n_films)`) record a budget of exactly zero, `r n0(n_bud_small)` a positive budget below the USD 10,000 floor, and `r n0(n_rev0)` zero revenue, while `roi` is missing on exactly those same zero-budget rows (`r toupper(as.character(same_rows))`). Identifiers are otherwise clean, with `r n0(n_dup_id)` duplicate IDs and only `r n0(n_dup_title)` repeated titles. Budgets below USD 10,000 and revenue of zero are therefore recoded as missing, and ROI is recomputed as `revenue_c / budget_c` rather than read from the file's own column. That missingness is not random: budget coverage is `r pct1(g_stat("Documentary", "cov_bud"))` in Documentary against `r pct1(g_stat("Adventure", "cov_bud"))` in Adventure, `r pct1(f_stat("Franchise", "cov_bud"))` for franchises against `r pct1(f_stat("Original", "cov_bud"))` for originals, and falls from `r pct1(d_stat(1950, "cov_bud"))` in the 1950s to `r pct1(d_stat(2000, "cov_bud"))` in the 2000s. After cleaning, `r n0(n_usable_bud)` films (`r pct1(pct_usable_bud)`) have a usable budget and `r n0(n_usable_roi)` (`r pct1(pct_usable_roi)`) a usable ROI.

## 1b Overall distribution of budget and ROI

```{r}
#| label: tbl-t1-summary
#| tbl-cap: "Distribution of production budget and ROI across the cleaned slate. Values are shown to three significant figures."

summ_row <- function(x, lab) {
  tibble(Variable = lab,
         N        = sum(!is.na(x)),
         Missing  = sum(is.na(x)),
         Mean     = mean(x, na.rm = TRUE),
         SD       = sd(x, na.rm = TRUE),
         Min      = min(x, na.rm = TRUE),
         Q1       = quantile(x, .25, na.rm = TRUE, names = FALSE),
         Median   = median(x, na.rm = TRUE),
         Q3       = quantile(x, .75, na.rm = TRUE, names = FALSE),
         Max      = max(x, na.rm = TRUE))
}

bind_rows(
  summ_row(films$budget_m, "Budget (USD m)"),
  summ_row(films$roi_c, "ROI (revenue / budget)"),
  summ_row(films$log10_budget, "log10 budget")
) |>
  gt() |>
  gt::fmt_number(
    columns = c(N, Missing),
    decimals = 0
  ) |>
  gt::fmt_number(
    columns = c(Mean, SD, Min, Q1, Median, Q3, Max),
    n_sigfig = 3
  )
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-t1-dist
#| fig-cap: "Overall distribution of production budget (A, B) and ROI (C, D). Dashed lines mark 1x return."
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 3.7

p1 <- films |> filter(!is.na(budget_c)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = budget_m)) + geom_histogram(bins = 40) +
  labs(title = "(A)", x = "Production budget (USD m)", y = "Count") + theme_minimal()

budget_curve <- tibble(
  log10_budget = seq(4, 9, length.out = 1000),
  density = dnorm(log10_budget, mean = mean(films$log10_budget, na.rm = TRUE), sd = sd(films$log10_budget, na.rm = TRUE))
)

p2 <- films |> filter(!is.na(log10_budget)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = log10_budget)) +
  geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density)), bins = 40) +
  geom_line(data = budget_curve, aes(x = log10_budget, y = density), linewidth = 1) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 4:9, labels = c("$10k", "$100k", "$1m", "$10m", "$100m", "$1b")) +
  labs(title = "(B)", x = "Production budget (log scale)", y = "Density") + theme_minimal()

p3 <- films |> filter(!is.na(roi_c), roi_c <= 15) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = roi_c)) + geom_histogram(bins = 40) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(title = "(C)", x = "ROI (revenue / budget)", y = "Count",
       subtitle = paste0(n_over15, " films exceeding 15x ROI omitted")) + theme_minimal()

p4 <- films |> filter(!is.na(log10_roi)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = log10_roi)) + geom_histogram(bins = 40) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = -2:2, labels = c("0.01x", "0.1x", "1x", "10x", "100x")) +
  labs(title = "(D)", x = "ROI (log scale)", y = "Count") + theme_minimal()

(p1 + p2) / (p3 + p4)
```

Panel A of @fig-t1-dist shows raw budget heavily skewed right: median budget is USD `r n1(med_budget_m)` million versus a mean of USD `r n1(mean_budget_m)` million and a maximum of USD `r n0(max_budget_m)` million. On a log-10 scale (Panel B), the distribution is approximately normal. Panel C shows ROI: median ROI is `r n2(med_roi)`, with IQR spanning `r n2(q1_roi)` to `r n2(q3_roi)`. About `r pct1(pct_flop)` of films sit below 1x ROI.

## 1c Slate composition by genre and franchise status


Horror is the cheapest focus genre (median USD `r n0(g_stat("Horror", "med_bud"))` m) and most lucrative (median ROI `r n2(g_stat("Horror", "med_roi"))`, `r pct1(g_stat("Horror", "rec_pct"))` recouped). Animation is expensive (median USD `r n0(g_stat("Animation", "med_bud"))` m) but reliable (`r pct1(g_stat("Animation", "rec_pct"))` recouped). Drama performs weakest (median ROI `r n2(g_stat("Drama", "med_roi"))`). Franchise films constitute `r pct1(100 * n_franchise / n_films)` of titles (@fig-t1-mix). Among complete cases (@tbl-t1-franchise), franchise titles take `r pct1(share_fs("Franchise", "budget_c"))` of budget while yielding `r pct1(share_fs("Franchise", "revenue_c"))` of revenue, outperforming originals on recoupment rate (`r pct1(f_stat("Franchise", "rec_pct"))` vs `r pct1(f_stat("Original", "rec_pct"))`).

## 1d Trends over time and summary for the Head of Production

```{r}
#| include: false
#| label: tbl-t1-decade
#| tbl-cap: "Slate composition by decade (decades with N >= 20)."

by_decade <- films |>
  filter(!is.na(release_year)) |>
  mutate(decade = paste0(floor(release_year / 10) * 10, "s")) |>
  group_by(decade) |>
  summarise(
    Years = paste0(min(release_year), "-", max(release_year)),
    Films = n(),
    `Median budget (USD m)` = round(median(budget_m, na.rm = TRUE), 1),
    `Median ROI`            = round(median(roi_c, na.rm = TRUE), 2),
    `% Franchise`           = round(100 * mean(franchise_status == "Franchise"), 1)
  ) |> filter(Films >= 20)

by_decade |> gt()|>
tab_options(
    table.font.size = "9pt",
    data_row.padding = px(3),
    column_labels.padding = px(3),
    table.width = pct(90)
)
dec_val <- function(d, col) by_decade[[col]][by_decade$decade == d]
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-t1-time
#| fig-cap: "Decadal trends in median budget (A), median ROI (B), and franchise share (C)."
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 2.2

by_time <- by_decade |> mutate(decade_num = as.numeric(sub("s", "", decade)))

q1 <- ggplot(by_time, aes(x = decade_num, y = `Median budget (USD m)`)) +
  geom_line(group = 1) + geom_point() + labs(title = "(A)", x = NULL) + theme_minimal()

q2 <- ggplot(by_time, aes(x = decade_num, y = `Median ROI`)) +
  geom_line(group = 1) + geom_point() + geom_hline(yintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(title = "(B)", x = NULL) + theme_minimal()

q3 <- ggplot(by_time, aes(x = decade_num, y = `% Franchise`)) +
  geom_line(group = 1) + geom_point() + labs(title = "(C)", x = NULL) + theme_minimal()

q1 + q2 + q3
```

Decadal figures show median budgets peaking at USD `r n0(max(by_decade$'Median budget (USD m)'))` million in the 1990s/2000s and stabilizing since. However, median ROI declined steadily from a peak of `r n2(max(by_decade$'Median ROI'))` in the 1970s to `r n2(min(by_decade$'Median ROI'))` in the 2000s (@fig-t1-time).

### Summary for the Head of Production

Only 77.7% of films have usable budgets and 66.9% usable ROI after treating placeholder financial values as missing. Coverage differs by genre, franchise status and decade, so comparisons may be affected by selection. Median budget is USD 24 million and median ROI is 2.30; 24.4% of observed films fail to recover their production budget. Medians and log scales better describe these skewed distributions than means.

Horror combines low budgets with relatively high recoupment, while franchises recover production budgets more often than originals (94.1% versus 74.2% among complete cases). These patterns support selective investigation of horror and franchise projects, rather than guaranteeing their success. Median ROI fell from 7.93 in the 1970s to 1.97 in the 2000s before recovering to 2.42 in the 2010s. Historical selection and unadjusted dollar values limit comparisons across decades; box-office revenue also excludes marketing, distribution and other costs.

# Task 2: Franchise vs. Original — Investment Strategy

## 2a Comparing the two budget distributions

```{r}
#| label: t2-setup
bud_t2 <- films |> filter(!is.na(budget_c))

n_f2 <- sum(bud_t2$franchise_status == "Franchise")
n_o2 <- sum(bud_t2$franchise_status == "Original")

bud_f2 <- bud_t2 |> filter(franchise_status == "Franchise") |> pull(budget_c)
bud_o2 <- bud_t2 |> filter(franchise_status == "Original")  |> pull(budget_c)

med_f2 <- median(bud_f2)
med_o2 <- median(bud_o2)
diff_obs2 <- med_f2 - med_o2

q_f2 <- quantile(bud_f2, c(.1, .25, .5, .75, .9), names = FALSE)
q_o2 <- quantile(bud_o2, c(.1, .25, .5, .75, .9), names = FALSE)

sd_logf2 <- sd(log10(bud_f2))
sd_logo2 <- sd(log10(bud_o2))
max_f2   <- max(bud_f2)
max_o2   <- max(bud_o2)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-t2-dist
#| fig-cap: "Log-10 production budget for the Franchise and Original groups across the whole dataset, with a fitted normal curve and a dashed line at each group median."
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 2.9
d2 <- bud_t2 |> mutate(log_bud = log10(budget_c))

curve_t2 <- bind_rows(
  tibble(franchise_status = "Franchise",
         log_bud = seq(4, 9, length.out = 500),
         density = dnorm(log_bud, mean = mean(log10(bud_f2)), sd = sd(log10(bud_f2)))),
  tibble(franchise_status = "Original",
         log_bud = seq(4, 9, length.out = 500),
         density = dnorm(log_bud, mean = mean(log10(bud_o2)), sd = sd(log10(bud_o2))))
)

med_t2 <- tibble(
  franchise_status = c("Franchise", "Original"),
  log_med = log10(c(med_f2, med_o2))
)

d2 |>
  ggplot(aes(x = log_bud)) +
  geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density)), bins = 25) +
  geom_line(data = curve_t2, aes(x = log_bud, y = density), linewidth = 1) +
  geom_vline(data = med_t2, aes(xintercept = log_med), linetype = "dashed") +
  facet_wrap(~ franchise_status) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 5:9,
                     labels = c("$100k", "$1m", "$10m", "$100m", "$1b")) +
  labs(x = "Production budget (log scale)", y = "Density") +
  theme_minimal()
```

@fig-t2-dist compares the `r n0(n_f2)` franchise and `r n0(n_o2)` original films that carry a usable budget. Both are strongly right-skewed in raw dollars and approximately symmetric on a log-10 scale, so the two groups differ mainly in location and spread, although originals show a longer lower tail. The fitted normal curve is a reasonable approximation in the centre of each distribution, but it overstates the franchise distribution above roughly USD 300 million, where the data are sparse.

Franchises are funded higher across the body of the distribution: the median is USD `r n1(med_f2 / 1e6)` million against USD `r n1(med_o2 / 1e6)` million, about `r n1(med_f2 / med_o2)` times as high, and the gap repeats at the lower quartile (USD `r n1(q_f2[2] / 1e6)` million against USD `r n1(q_o2[2] / 1e6)` million), the upper quartile (USD `r n1(q_f2[4] / 1e6)` million against USD `r n1(q_o2[4] / 1e6)` million) and the 90th percentile (USD `r n0(q_f2[5] / 1e6)` million against USD `r n0(q_o2[5] / 1e6)` million). Spread runs the other way: originals are the more dispersed group on the log scale, with a standard deviation of `r n2(sd_logo2)` against `r n2(sd_logf2)`; they reach lower at the bottom, with a tenth percentile of USD `r n1(q_o2[1] / 1e6)` million against USD `r n1(q_f2[1] / 1e6)` million; and the single largest budget in the file belongs to one original film, at USD `r n0(max_o2 / 1e6)` million against USD `r n0(max_f2 / 1e6)` million for the largest franchise.

## 2b A 95% interval estimate for the difference in medians

```{r}
#| label: t2-boot
set.seed(2420)
boot_diff <- replicate(20000,
  median(sample(bud_f2, n_f2, replace = TRUE)) -
  median(sample(bud_o2, n_o2, replace = TRUE))
)

boot_se2 <- sd(boot_diff)
boot_ci2 <- quantile(boot_diff, c(.025, .975), names = FALSE)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-t2-boot
#| tbl-cap: "Bootstrap interval estimate for the difference in median budget (Franchise minus Original), from 20,000 resamples drawn within each group."
tibble(
  Quantity = c("Observed difference (USD m)",
               "Bootstrap standard error (USD m)",
               "95% percentile interval (USD m)"),
  Estimate = c(n1(diff_obs2 / 1e6),
               n2(boot_se2 / 1e6),
               paste0(n1(boot_ci2[1] / 1e6), " to ", n1(boot_ci2[2] / 1e6)))
) |> gt()
```

The observed difference in median budget, franchise minus original, is USD `r n1(diff_obs2 / 1e6)` million. Resampling 20,000 times within each group gives a bootstrap standard error of USD `r n2(boot_se2 / 1e6)` million and a 95% percentile interval of USD `r n1(boot_ci2[1] / 1e6)` million to USD `r n1(boot_ci2[2] / 1e6)` million (@tbl-t2-boot). The 95% bootstrap interval lies entirely above zero, providing evidence that the population median budget is higher for franchise films than for original films. It is nonetheless wide relative to the estimate, which is expected given only `r n0(n_f2)` franchise films and a heavily skewed budget variable, so the gap is better read as a substantial difference in the median budget than as a precise figure.

## 2c Does the evidence support leadership's concern?

```{r}
#| label: t2-shares
cc_t2 <- films |> filter(!is.na(budget_c), !is.na(revenue_c))

n_cc2     <- nrow(cc_t2)
pct_excl2 <- 100 * (1 - n_cc2 / nrow(bud_t2))

share_n_f2   <- 100 * sum(cc_t2$franchise_status == "Franchise") / n_cc2
share_bud_f2 <- 100 * sum(cc_t2$budget_c[cc_t2$franchise_status == "Franchise"]) / sum(cc_t2$budget_c)
share_rev_f2 <- 100 * sum(cc_t2$revenue_c[cc_t2$franchise_status == "Franchise"]) / sum(cc_t2$revenue_c)
rec_f2 <- 100 * mean(cc_t2$roi_c[cc_t2$franchise_status == "Franchise"] >= 1)
rec_o2 <- 100 * mean(cc_t2$roi_c[cc_t2$franchise_status == "Original"]  >= 1)

share_small_f2     <- 100 * mean(bud_f2 < 1e7)
share_small_o2     <- 100 * mean(bud_o2 < 1e7)
share_small20_o2   <- 100 * mean(bud_o2 < 2e7)

hor_o2     <- cc_t2 |> filter(primary_genre == "Horror", franchise_status == "Original")
rec_hor_o2 <- 100 * mean(hor_o2$roi_c >= 1)
med_hor_o2 <- median(hor_o2$budget_c)
```

The cost half of the concern holds up. Franchises are funded higher at the median, at both quartiles and at the 90th percentile, and the interval in @tbl-t2-boot provides evidence that franchise films have a higher population median budget. A typical original film is smaller than a typical franchise film at every quantile reported, so "the original slate is cheaper" is correct as stated.

What does not hold up is the description of that slate as "mostly small, low-budget projects". Only `r pct1(share_small_o2)` of original films carry a budget below USD 10 million, against `r pct1(share_small_f2)` of franchises, and even on the more generous reading of "small" as under USD 20 million, fewer than half of originals qualify (`r pct1(share_small20_o2)`). The middle half of the original slate runs from USD `r n1(q_o2[2] / 1e6)` million to USD `r n1(q_o2[4] / 1e6)` million, which is mid-budget rather than micro-budget. Originals are also the more dispersed group, as @fig-t2-dist shows, but that extra spread sits at the cheap end of the range rather than the top.

The revenue premise is not supported. Among the `r n0(n_cc2)` films with complete financials, franchise titles are only `r pct1(share_n_f2)` of the slate, take `r pct1(share_bud_f2)` of production budget and generate `r pct1(share_rev_f2)` of revenue. A group producing `r pct1(share_rev_f2)` of revenue is a valuable group, but it is not carrying the studio, and describing it that way overstates both its current weight and the risk of shifting the slate towards originals. What the franchise group genuinely provides is reliability rather than volume: `r pct1(rec_f2)` of franchise titles recoup their production budget against `r pct1(rec_o2)` of originals.

## 2d Recommended strategy

**Keep the franchise pipeline.** Franchise titles convert `r pct1(share_bud_f2)` of production budget into `r pct1(share_rev_f2)` of revenue and recoup at `r pct1(rec_f2)`, against `r pct1(rec_o2)` for originals. Cutting the pipeline to make room for originals would trade a dependable engine for a cheaper but more variable investment, and nothing in the evidence requires that trade.

**Grow the original slate selectively.** The comparison does not say originals are a bad investment; it says they are cheaper and more variable. The lowest-risk way to add original volume is to fund it where low cost and high recoupment already coincide. Horror is the clearest case: original horror films recoup at `r pct1(rec_hor_o2)`, well above the `r pct1(rec_o2)` that originals achieve as a whole, on a median budget of only USD `r n0(med_hor_o2 / 1e6)` million. Mid-budget Drama, by contrast, is the weakest category in the slate. Pilot a small number of titles before committing a full slate.

**Balance.** Concretely, keep franchise spending at roughly its current level in dollar terms and direct incremental spend to originals, expanding that program only once the pilot titles recoup at rates approaching the original horror benchmark of `r pct1(rec_hor_o2)`; note that pilot sample sizes will be small and can only provide directional evidence. That preserves the dependable half of the slate while buying evidence on the more variable half, rather than committing to it on the strength of the budget gap alone.

**Caveats.** The comparison is descriptive rather than causal: genre mix and release era differ between the two groups and neither is controlled for here, so the budget gap cannot be read as the price of the franchise label. The revenue shares and recoupment rates are complete-case figures covering `r n0(n_cc2)` of the `r n0(nrow(bud_t2))` films with a usable budget, leaving `r pct1(pct_excl2)` of that group excluded; if missing revenue is concentrated among weaker performers, the recoupment rates reported here are optimistic. Revenue in the file is also gross rather than net of distribution, marketing and participation, so recoupment measures whether a film matched its production budget, not whether it made money for the studio.

# Task 3: Modelling Budgets & Downside Risk

## 3a Modelling Universal Pictures’ production budgets

```{r}
#| include: false
library(tidyverse)

movies <- read_csv("data/movies.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

universal_budget <- movies |>
  filter(
    primary_company == "Universal Pictures",
    is.finite(budget),
    budget >= 10000
  ) |>
  mutate(budget_millions = budget / 1e6)

# Check the filtered data
universal_budget |>
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    min_budget = min(budget),
    median_budget = median(budget),
    mean_budget = mean(budget),
    max_budget = max(budget)
  )
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-t3-budget-dist
#| fig-cap: "Distribution of production budgets for Universal Pictures films."
ggplot(universal_budget, aes(x = budget_millions)) +
  geom_histogram(
    aes(y = after_stat(density)),
    bins = 25,
    fill = "skyblue",
    colour = "white"
  ) +
  geom_density(colour = "red", linewidth = 1) +
  labs(
    title = "Budget Distribution of Universal Pictures Films",
    x = "Budget (US$ millions)",
    y = "Density"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r}
universal_budget |>
  summarise(
    skewness = mean(
      (budget_millions - mean(budget_millions))^3
    ) / sd(budget_millions)^3
  )
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-t3-aic
#| tbl-cap: "AIC comparison of candidate models for Universal Pictures production budgets."
library(fitdistrplus)

budget <- universal_budget$budget_millions

fit_normal <- fitdist(budget, "norm")
fit_lognormal <- fitdist(budget, "lnorm")
fit_gamma <- fitdist(budget, "gamma")

aic_results <- tibble(
  Distribution = c("Normal", "Log-normal", "Gamma"),
  AIC = c(
    fit_normal$aic,
    fit_lognormal$aic,
    fit_gamma$aic
  )
) |>
  arrange(AIC)

knitr::kable(aic_results, digits = 1)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-t3-budget-qq
#| fig-cap: "Q–Q plots comparing normal, log-normal and gamma models for Universal Pictures production budgets."
par(mfrow = c(1, 3))

qqcomp(
  fit_normal,
  main = "Normal"
)

qqcomp(
  fit_lognormal,
  main = "Log-normal"
)

qqcomp(
  fit_gamma,
  main = "Gamma"
)

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

After excluding invalid and placeholder budget values below US\$10,000, 243 Universal Pictures films remained. The budget distribution (@fig-t3-budget-dist) was positively skewed, with a sample skewness of 1.57, suggesting that a symmetric normal distribution may be unsuitable.

Three candidate distributions were fitted: normal, log-normal and gamma. The gamma distribution achieved the lowest AIC (2320.1), compared with 2349.2 for the log-normal distribution and 2454.1 for the normal distribution (@tbl-t3-aic). The Q–Q plots (@fig-t3-budget-qq) also suggest that the gamma model provides the closest overall fit, although some deviations remain in the upper tail. Therefore, among the three candidates, the gamma distribution is the preferred model for describing Universal Pictures film budgets.

## 3b Estimating the 25th percentile of Action ROI

```{r}
films |>
  summarise(
    total_rows = n(),
    has_genre = "primary_genre" %in% names(films),
    has_budget = "budget" %in% names(films),
    has_revenue = "revenue" %in% names(films)
  )
```

```{r}
action_films <- films |>
  filter(
    primary_genre == "Action",
    is.finite(budget),
    budget >= 10000,
    is.finite(revenue),
    revenue > 0
  ) |>
  mutate(roi_calc = revenue / budget) |>
  filter(is.finite(roi_calc))

action_films |>
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    roi_q25 = quantile(roi_calc, 0.25),
    roi_median = median(roi_calc),
    roi_min = min(roi_calc),
    roi_max = max(roi_calc)
  )
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-t3-roi-ci
#| tbl-cap: "Estimated 25th percentile of Action-film ROI and 95% confidence intervals."
set.seed(2420)

# Point estimate
q25_hat <- quantile(action_films$roi_calc, 0.25)

# Method 1: Bootstrap percentile interval
B <- 5000

boot_q25 <- replicate(B, {
  boot_sample <- sample(
    action_films$roi_calc,
    size = nrow(action_films),
    replace = TRUE
  )
  quantile(boot_sample, 0.25)
})

boot_ci <- quantile(boot_q25, c(0.025, 0.975))

# Method 2: Order-statistic interval
x <- sort(action_films$roi_calc)
n <- length(x)

alpha <- 0.05
lower_index <- qbinom(alpha / 2, n, 0.25)
upper_index <- qbinom(1 - alpha / 2, n, 0.25) + 1

# Keep indices within valid sample positions
lower_index <- max(1, lower_index)
upper_index <- min(n, upper_index)

order_ci <- c(
  lower = x[lower_index],
  upper = x[upper_index]
)

# Display results
tibble(
  Method = c("Bootstrap percentile", "Order statistic"),
  Estimate = rep(as.numeric(q25_hat), 2),
  `Lower 95% CI` = c(boot_ci[1], order_ci[1]),
  `Upper 95% CI` = c(boot_ci[2], order_ci[2])
) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```

For Action films across all studios, the estimated 25th percentile of ROI was 0.907. The bootstrap percentile 95% confidence interval was \[0.798, 1.052\], while the order-statistic interval was \[0.794, 1.072\]. Both methods produced the same point estimate, with the order-statistic interval slightly wider. The results suggest that the lower quartile of Action-film ROI is close to 1, although uncertainty remains around this benchmark.

## 3c Comparison of the percentile estimators

Both methods estimate the 25th percentile as 0.907 and give similar 95% confidence intervals (@tbl-t3-roi-ci). The order-statistic interval is slightly wider. The bootstrap method resamples the observed films, whereas the order-statistic method uses ranked observations and binomial probabilities to obtain interval bounds. Both intervals include 1, so the population lower quartile could lie on either side of the production-budget recoupment benchmark.

## 3d Recommendation for Finance

For the budget simulator, we recommend the gamma distribution for Universal Pictures’ production budgets because it has the lowest AIC among the three candidates and is supported by the Q–Q diagnostics. This model provides a historical benchmark rather than a guarantee of Meridian’s future cost structure.

For the Action slate, Finance should plan around a lower-quartile ROI of approximately 0.91: about one quarter of films in the observed sample earned less than 91 cents in worldwide box-office revenue per dollar of production budget. The two 95% confidence intervals are approximately 0.80–1.05 and 0.79–1.07, indicating uncertainty around the 1x production-budget recoupment benchmark. This figure describes the lower quarter of the observed revenue-to-budget ratios and should not be interpreted as a prediction for an individual film. ROI is calculated using reported worldwide box-office revenue and production budget; it does not account for marketing, distribution or other costs. Missing financial records and the historical nature of the sample should also be considered when applying these findings to future greenlighting decisions.

# Task 4: Building a Greenlight Risk Model

## 4a Outcome and analysis sample

A flop is defined as worldwide box-office revenue below production budget (ROI \< 1). Logistic regression suits this binary outcome and constrains fitted probabilities to 0–1; ordinary linear regression does not, while Poisson regression models counts. Budgets below USD 10,000 and non-positive revenues were excluded as missing placeholders. We used films released by 2016 in Meridian's five focus genres, retaining complete predictor records. The resulting 2,256 films included 574 flops (25.4%). Results apply to this observed financial-data subset, not all releases.

```{r}
#| label: t4-data
#| include: false
library(tidyverse)
library(brms)

t4_data <- read_csv("data/movies.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  filter(release_year <= 2016, budget >= 10000, revenue > 0) |>
  mutate(
    roi_c = revenue / budget,
    flop = as.integer(roi_c < 1),
    log_budget = log(budget),
    primary_genre = factor(primary_genre),
    franchise_status = factor(franchise_status,
                              levels = c("Original", "Franchise"))
  ) |>
  drop_na(primary_genre, franchise_status, log_budget, cast_size) |>
  filter(primary_genre %in%
           c("Action", "Comedy", "Drama", "Horror", "Animation")) |>
  mutate(
    primary_genre = relevel(droplevels(primary_genre), ref = "Drama"),
    cast_10 = cast_size / 10
  )

# Reproduce the original stratified 80/20 split
set.seed(24205242)
t4_train_ids <- t4_data |>
  group_by(flop) |>
  slice_sample(prop = 0.8) |>
  ungroup() |>
  pull(id)
t4_train <- t4_data |> filter(id %in% t4_train_ids)
t4_test <- t4_data |> filter(!id %in% t4_train_ids)
```

## 4b Frequentist and Bayesian models

Both models used genre, franchise status, natural-log budget and cast size per ten actors, with Drama and Original as reference categories. A stratified 80/20 split (seed 24205242) produced 1,804 training and 452 test films. Recorded cast size approximates planned cast size: use at greenlight requires a credible advance estimate, rather than information learned after release. We assume independent film outcomes and additive, linear effects of log budget and cast size on log-odds; related franchise films may challenge independence.

```{r}
#| label: t4-frequentist
#| include: false
t4_freq <- glm(
  flop ~ primary_genre + franchise_status + log_budget + cast_10,
  data = t4_train, family = binomial(link = "logit")
)
t4_coef <- coef(summary(t4_freq))
t4_or <- data.frame(
  Term = rownames(t4_coef),
  OR = exp(t4_coef[, "Estimate"]),
  Lower_95 = exp(t4_coef[, "Estimate"] - 1.96 * t4_coef[, "Std. Error"]),
  Upper_95 = exp(t4_coef[, "Estimate"] + 1.96 * t4_coef[, "Std. Error"])
)
```

```{r}
#| label: t4-bayesian
#| include: false
#| cache: true
# Fit from the submitted source without requiring an external RDS file
t4_bayes <- brm(
  formula = flop ~ primary_genre + franchise_status + log_budget + cast_10,
  data = t4_train,
  family = bernoulli(link = "logit"),
  prior = c(
    prior(normal(0, 1), class = "b"),
    prior(normal(0, 2.5), class = "Intercept")
  ),
  chains = 4, iter = 4000, warmup = 1000,
  cores = 2, seed = 24205242
)
t4_bcoef <- fixef(t4_bayes)
t4_draws <- posterior::as_draws_df(t4_bayes)
t4_post_prob <- mean(t4_draws$b_franchise_statusFranchise < 0)

# Sampling diagnostics; retain calculations without large diagnostic output
t4_sampler <- rstan::get_sampler_params(t4_bayes$fit, inc_warmup = FALSE)
t4_divergences <- sum(vapply(t4_sampler,
  function(x) sum(x[, "divergent__"]), numeric(1)))
t4_depth_hits <- sum(vapply(t4_sampler,
  function(x) sum(x[, "treedepth__"] >= 10), numeric(1)))
t4_max_rhat <- max(
  posterior::summarise_draws(posterior::as_draws_array(t4_bayes))$rhat,
  na.rm = TRUE
)
```

Weakly informative priors were Normal(0, 1) for slopes and Normal(0, 2.5) for the internally centred intercept, on the log-odds scale. A slope prior places about 95% probability on odds ratios between 0.14 and 7.10 per predictor unit. Four chains yielded 12,000 post-warmup draws. Maximum R-hat was `r sprintf("%.3f", t4_max_rhat)`, with `r t4_divergences` divergences and `r t4_depth_hits` maximum-tree-depth hits; the inspected trace plots showed good mixing.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-t4-models
#| tbl-cap: "Adjusted odds ratios: frequentist 95% confidence intervals and Bayesian 95% credible intervals."
#| echo: false
t4_terms <- c("primary_genreAction", "primary_genreAnimation",
              "primary_genreComedy", "primary_genreHorror",
              "franchise_statusFranchise", "log_budget", "cast_10")
t4_labels <- c("Action vs Drama", "Animation vs Drama", "Comedy vs Drama",
               "Horror vs Drama", "Franchise vs Original",
               "Log budget (+1)", "Cast size (+10)")
t4_f <- t4_or[match(t4_terms, t4_or$Term), ]
t4_b <- t4_bcoef[t4_terms, , drop = FALSE]
t4_fmt <- function(est, lo, hi) sprintf("%.2f (%.2f–%.2f)", est, lo, hi)
t4_model_table <- tibble(
  Predictor = t4_labels,
  `Frequentist OR (95% CI)` = t4_fmt(t4_f$OR, t4_f$Lower_95, t4_f$Upper_95),
  `Bayesian OR (95% CrI)` = t4_fmt(exp(t4_b[, "Estimate"]),
                                  exp(t4_b[, "Q2.5"]), exp(t4_b[, "Q97.5"]))
)
knitr::kable(t4_model_table)
```

The two approaches agree closely (@tbl-t4-models). Holding other predictors fixed, franchise films have lower flop odds: OR 0.24 (CI 0.12–0.48), versus Bayesian OR 0.27 (CrI 0.14–0.48). Ten additional cast members are associated with OR 0.81 under both models (approximately 0.75–0.87). These are associations, not causal effects or percentage-point probability changes. All 12,000 sampled franchise coefficients were negative, estimating the posterior probability of lower franchise flop odds as approximately 100%, conditional on the model and priors. Comedy is borderline: its frequentist interval narrowly excludes 1, whereas its Bayesian interval includes 1. A confidence interval describes repeated-sampling coverage; a credible interval describes posterior uncertainty under the specified model.

## 4c Test-set performance

We used the training flop proportion (`r sprintf("%.3f", mean(t4_train$flop))`) as a screening threshold, with 0.50 as a benchmark. This deliberately gives more attention to possible flops, which are the minority class. The threshold was not optimised on the test set and does not represent a proven optimal business cost trade-off.

```{r}
#| label: t4-evaluation
#| include: false
t4_prob_freq <- predict(t4_freq, newdata = t4_test, type = "response")
t4_prob_bayes <- colMeans(posterior_epred(t4_bayes, newdata = t4_test))
t4_threshold <- mean(t4_train$flop)
t4_metrics <- function(prob, actual, threshold) {
  predicted <- as.integer(prob >= threshold)
  TP <- sum(predicted == 1 & actual == 1)
  TN <- sum(predicted == 0 & actual == 0)
  FP <- sum(predicted == 1 & actual == 0)
  FN <- sum(predicted == 0 & actual == 1)
  data.frame(Threshold = threshold, TP = TP, TN = TN, FP = FP, FN = FN,
    Accuracy = (TP + TN) / length(actual),
    Sensitivity = TP / (TP + FN), Specificity = TN / (TN + FP),
    Precision = ifelse(TP + FP > 0, TP / (TP + FP), NA_real_))
}
t4_performance <- bind_rows(
  t4_metrics(t4_prob_freq, t4_test$flop, 0.5) |> mutate(Model = "Frequentist"),
  t4_metrics(t4_prob_freq, t4_test$flop, t4_threshold) |> mutate(Model = "Frequentist"),
  t4_metrics(t4_prob_bayes, t4_test$flop, 0.5) |> mutate(Model = "Bayesian"),
  t4_metrics(t4_prob_bayes, t4_test$flop, t4_threshold) |> mutate(Model = "Bayesian")
)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-t4-performance
#| tbl-cap: "Held-out performance (%); flop is the positive outcome. A dash denotes undefined precision."
#| echo: false
t4_perf_table <- t4_performance |>
  dplyr::select(Model, Threshold, Accuracy, Sensitivity, Specificity, Precision) |>
  mutate(Threshold = sprintf("%.3f", Threshold),
    across(c(Accuracy, Sensitivity, Specificity, Precision),
      ~ ifelse(is.na(.x), "—", sprintf("%.1f", 100 * .x))))
knitr::kable(t4_perf_table)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-t4-confusion
#| tbl-cap: "Bayesian screening confusion matrix: rows are actual outcomes; columns are predictions."
#| echo: false
t4_predicted <- as.integer(t4_prob_bayes >= t4_threshold)
t4_confusion <- table(
  Actual = factor(t4_test$flop, levels = c(0, 1), labels = c("Non-flop", "Flop")),
  Predicted = factor(t4_predicted, levels = c(0, 1), labels = c("Non-flop", "Flop"))
)
knitr::kable(t4_confusion)
```

At 0.50 both models predict no flops: 74.6% accuracy merely matches always predicting non-flop. At the lower threshold, the Bayesian model detects 86 of 115 flops (74.8% sensitivity), but falsely flags 181 non-flops; precision is only 32.2%. It therefore supports further review rather than automatic rejection. Neither discrimination nor future performance is guaranteed by these results from one random split.

## 4d Pitches and advice to the Head of Production

```{r}
#| label: t4-pitches
#| include: false
t4_pitches <- tibble(
  Pitch = c("Original horror", "Original drama", "Franchise action"),
  primary_genre = factor(c("Horror", "Drama", "Action"),
                         levels = levels(t4_train$primary_genre)),
  franchise_status = factor(c("Original", "Original", "Franchise"),
                            levels = levels(t4_train$franchise_status)),
  budget_m = c(10, 25, 80), planned_cast = c(15, 25, 40)
) |>
  mutate(log_budget = log(budget_m * 1e6), cast_10 = planned_cast / 10)
t4_pitch_draws <- posterior_epred(t4_bayes, newdata = t4_pitches)
t4_pitch_results <- t4_pitches |>
  dplyr::select(Pitch, budget_m, planned_cast) |>
  mutate(Flop_probability = colMeans(t4_pitch_draws),
    Lower_95 = apply(t4_pitch_draws, 2, quantile, probs = 0.025),
    Upper_95 = apply(t4_pitch_draws, 2, quantile, probs = 0.975))
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-t4-pitches
#| tbl-cap: "Hypothetical pitches: posterior mean flop probabilities and 95% credible intervals."
#| echo: false
t4_pitch_table <- t4_pitch_results |>
  transmute(Pitch, `Budget (USD m)` = budget_m, Cast = planned_cast,
    `Flop % (95% CrI)` = t4_fmt(100 * Flop_probability,
                                100 * Lower_95, 100 * Upper_95),
    Recommendation = c("Conditional go", "Hold for review", "Conditional go"))
knitr::kable(t4_pitch_table)
```

**Management summary.** Provisionally support the horror and franchise-action pitches, subject to normal commercial and budget checks. Hold the original drama for closer review of its costs and revenue assumptions. The intervals quantify uncertainty in each estimated probability, not the outcome of one film. This model is a screening aid: many flags are false alarms, and lower flop probability does not imply higher profit or smaller financial exposure. Results concern five genres with reported financial data; historical selection, franchise dependence and uncertain planned cast sizes limit generalisation. Box office is not studio receipts, and the outcome excludes marketing, distribution and other costs. No pitch is guaranteed to be profitable.
